Except the composition of the U.S. economy is changing. When we lose jobs, they are good manufacturing and tech jobs. When we gain jobs they are in the service and retail sectors; these sectors account for the two largest shares of low-wage workers.

When, as was the case in the past, only a small portion of jobs pay minimum (or near minimum) wage, your argument makes sense--let the kids do the shitty jobs. As the number of jobs that pay minimum (or near minimum) hourly wages increases as a portion of the economy, or in the absence of sufficient higher-paying jobs to sustain adults, this argument breaks down.

Only about 25% of workers earning the federal minimum were teenagers in 2014. In the same year, half a million people with college degrees were working minimum wage jobs (I saw one article that said three quarters of a million in 2013, the figures you find vary). This isn't a reflection of those workers' preferences.

If the minimum wage had been increased in line with both inflation and increases in productivity since 1968, it would be at least $15, the fact that it has not is emblematic of a shift in the capital/labor split, and when capital's share of income grows, inequality of wealth grows, and disparities in political power between elites and average citizens are amplified, allowing those who are already wealthy and powerful to control government (and through it, the economy) for their own advantage.

Even a $10 minimum wage would not be sufficient to lift a vast number of working families out of poverty, especially considering the move towards so-called labor flexibility (part time workers instead of full time workers, irregular shifts, etc.) which has lead to chronic underemployment and has had a devastating effect on the family. Most low wage workers are not teenagers, but adults who shoulder a significant portion (if not all) of the bread-winning responsibilities for their families (many of these people have college degrees, even advanced degrees, but can't find better jobs). These low wages and part time employment schemes, designed to maximize corporate profits and shareholder returns cost all of us in tax dollars, as those workers are subsidized by the government. Medicaid, food stamps, public housing, etc.

While it may be true that some jobs will be lost if the minimum were increased, there isn't reason to think this would be widespread. Wal Mart, for example, makes well over $10k a year in profits per associate, and could absorb the increase in the price of labor without making any other changes. While fast food franchisees make thin margins, the franchisers that sell them everything from their signage, tables, chairs and decorations to their food are making huge profits, and could charge franchisees less, enabling them to pay higher wages and stay in the black. The loss of jobs from businesses that truly cannot afford the labor at the minimum cost would be offset by the jobs created by the increase in demand for goods and services by those workers lifted out of poverty, who can now spend more money.

While prices for goods and services may increase slightly, there is no reason to think they would increase dramatically. As noted before, the largest employers who pay the minimum wage make plenty of profits to absorb higher costs. In Denmark, McDonald's workers make something like $20 an hour, and it should be noted that a Big Mac there is only $0.20-$0.25 more expensive than it is in the U.S. (which is a consequence of people being significantly better payed across the economy, and therefore willing to pay a little more--it has nothing to do with costs, that isn't how prices are set).

Any such increase in price would reflect a change in the price that creates maximum profits. Unless you think McDonald's is a poorly run corporation, you should understand that prices are being set now to maximize profits; if they could raise the price and make more money, they would have already done so. Even if low wage workers would be willing to spend a little more, there's no reason to think people higher in the economy would suddenly see more utility in a Big Mac. Furthermore, every competitor would have to raise their prices likewise, if McDonald's tried to raise prices to maintain profit levels, Wendy's might not, and Wendy's would see an increase in market share, and McDonald's profits would fall. The industries that pay minimum wage are highly competitive.

The $15 dollar number may not be the perfect number, but if we ask for that, we can be sure powerful interests will influence Congress to land at a lower number, and this would be true no matter what is asked for. You don't start negotiations with no where to compromise.

Not only does forcing the capital/labor split back towards labor a little bit make good economic sense, but it is the just thing to do for American workers, who are working longer hours for lower wages than their parents and grandparents did.

These are roughly the arguments put forth by economist, Chancellors Professor of Public Policy at U.C. Berkeley, and former Secretary of Labor, Robert Reich. They have been echoed closely by Nobel Prize winner Joseph Stiglitz.
